\section[la carrera]{la carrera — the career; the degree; the race}

\label{lesson:ES-C595-carrera}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to run, then the Spanish for to manage.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la carrera}
\textbf{la carrera} — \textquotedblleft{}the career; the degree; the race\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tiene una larga carrera en la empresa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She has a long career in the company.}
\end{quote}

In Spain \emph{hacer una carrera} is to study for a degree.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{carrera} is usually traced to Late Latin \emph{(via) carraria} 'cart road', built on \emph{carrus} 'a wagon' (Lewis \& Short); a road became a race and then a career.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la carrera}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la carrera}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la carrera}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to run, then the Spanish for to manage, then say \emph{la carrera} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la carrera mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The career; the degree; the race\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ascender]{ascender — to be promoted; to rise}

\label{lesson:ES-C595-ascender}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to manage, then the Spanish for the career.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ascender}
\textbf{ascender} — \textquotedblleft{}to be promoted; to rise\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ascendió a directora en dos años.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She was promoted to director in two years.}
\end{quote}

Stem change e$\to$ie: \emph{asciendo}. \emph{Ascender a} + post.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ascender} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{ascendere} 'to climb up', built from \emph{ad} and \emph{scandere} 'to climb' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to manage, then the Spanish for the career, then say \emph{ascender} again
\end{itemize}

\section[el mérito]{el mérito — the merit, the credit}

\label{lesson:ES-C595-merito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the career, then the Spanish for to be promoted.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el mérito}
\textbf{el mérito} — \textquotedblleft{}the merit, the credit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Todo el mérito es suyo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{All the credit is hers.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Tener mérito} — to deserve credit.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mérito} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{meritum} 'what one deserves', the participle of \emph{merere} 'to earn' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[ambicioso]{ambicioso — ambitious}

\label{lesson:ES-C595-ambicioso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to be promoted, then the Spanish for the merit.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ambicioso}
\textbf{ambicioso} — \textquotedblleft{}ambitious\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Es un proyecto muy ambicioso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{It is a very ambitious project.}
\end{quote}

It can be good or bad: \emph{una persona ambiciosa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ambicioso} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{ambitiosus} (EtymDB), built on \emph{ambitio} 'a going round to ask for votes', from \emph{ambire} 'to go round'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[triunfar]{triunfar — to succeed, to triumph}

\label{lesson:ES-C595-triunfar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the merit, then the Spanish for ambitious.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: triunfar}
\textbf{triunfar} — \textquotedblleft{}to succeed, to triumph\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Quiere triunfar en su profesión.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He wants to succeed in his profession.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Triunfar en la vida} — to be a success in life.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{triunfar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{triumphare} 'to hold a victory procession', built on \emph{triumphus} 'triumph' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
